rv.q: For a show of and about so many bad jokes, that’s one hell of a punchline.
The Bedwetter in its current awkward state does have charm; Bebe Neuwirth drawls “There is no God”; it’s sold out; it’s good.
Too often the rest of “The Bedwetter,” at least when aiming for tears, feels merely wet.
So why does it come off so slight and tentative?
The Bedwetter is also an insightful and moving depiction of dysfunctional family dynamics, a little girl's triumph over insecurity and the healing power of comedy.

So it comes as a bit of a surprise that this new musical adapted from comedian/actress Sarah Silverman’s best-selling memoir emerges as not only one of the funniest but also the sweetest shows in town.

All in all, The Bedwetter is an amiable summer diversion, adeptly directed by Anne Kauffman and performed in a loose, affable style with an unimpeachable message of acceptance for everyone, warts and all.
It’s refreshing to see these preteen girls rendered with a respect to their feelings and experiences.
The Bedwetter ultimately delivers a message about the powers of streaming your truth.

The musical features excellent writing and cutting zingers, alongside a sketchier story and character progression, raising more questions than answers about the family, its many traumas, tensions and fractures, and what Silverman herself went through and how it affected her.

Bathos overtakes “The Bedwetter,” and somehow all that sticky sentiment delivers an antidote that not only cures Sarah of her bedwetting but it gets Mom out of bed and turns Dad into a good guy, and even Grandma manages to cut her alcohol consumption in half.
But this combination proves to be just a little less delicious than usual in the new musical "The Bedwetter," now premiering at the Atlantic Theater Company under Anne Kauffman's direction.
The audience comes away in love with the very human, flawed and guilty characters expoosed in Silverman’s autobiographical story.
Not only is The Bedwetter inventive, it is a beautiful, provocative showcase of dynamic female characters.
With dirty jokes, dramatic fizz, and a heartwarming takeaway, The Bedwetter is utterly delightful and sure to be a crowd-pleaser.
In this uneven production, as director Anne Kauffman has discovered, a depressed kid with a foul mouth makes for a problematic protagonist.

The songs by Silverman and Schlesinger (with contributions by composer David Yazbek) are sometimes hysterically rude and dirty, but others feel like fillers to give every minor character a moment to sing.
The sad truth is that this tale of a young girl’s trauma is only intermittently capable of generating amusement on its own.
If that’s not the case, this two-hour show may be tougher to swallow than those dancing Xanax tablets and the nonstop gratuitous profanity.
Her alcoholic grandmother (a pitch-perfect Bebe Neuwirth) attempts to be supportive, but can’t deliver an unqualified compliment, except of Sarah’s perfectly mixed Manhattan.

cn.t: Sarah Silverman's memoir becomes an uneven but charming musical that mixes vulgar humor with genuine heart. Critics praise its wit and emotional depth, though some find it struggles to balance crude comedy with serious themes of childhood trauma.
